documents: Published paper: Harmon et al. (2022) Surface deployment of DAS systems: Coupling strategies and comparisons to geophone data. Near Surface Geophysics 20:465-477 (PDF)

entry.evidence: However, proper mechanical coupling between the fibre and the ground is still a challenge for temporary surface deployments.

steps.action: Cite prior surface-deployed DAS tests (sandbag weighting, frozen trench) that compared DAS with geophones and found improved signal recovery.
steps.quote: compare favourably with multichannel geophone data (Spikes et al., 2019)

steps.action: Pose the question of whether rapid, temporary surface DAS deployments are viable, and which coupling strategy is best.
steps.quote: further investigation into the viability of rapid and temporary surface deployments of optical fibre and optimal deployment strategies is warranted

steps.action: Design a comparison of four coupling strategies against a co-located 24-channel vertical geophone line, with an inverted-L fibre geometry that records two orthogonal horizontal components.
steps.quote: In this study, we examine four different surface coupling strategies for DAS systems

steps.action: Use the group's own differential-phase DAS interrogator (IMZI, 4 m gauge length, 0.30 m channels, 0.5 ms sampling) on standard SMF-28 tight-buffer fibre.
steps.quote: we used the University of Southampton proprietary designed differential phase interrogator

steps.action: Set the field conditions: a first shot series with uncoupled fibre, then a second with fibre pinned by DAviS couplers, weighted by carpet, and weighted by a sandbag; hammer shots every 2 m.
steps.quote: We tested four different approaches of coupling the fibre to the ground during two shot series experiments.

steps.action: Record DAS and geophone data, repeating the coupled experiment with geophones tilted about 30 degrees so that a horizontal component can be estimated (Eq. 1).
steps.quote: The multi-channel data using the two different geophone orientations were used to estimate the horizontal ground motion

steps.action: Propagate a ±15° uncertainty in the geophone tilt angle into the estimated horizontal waveforms, citing published evidence that tilted geophones remain valid below a critical angle.
steps.quote: We estimate the error in the ∼30◦ deployment angle at ±15◦ and use this error range to quantify the error in the waveforms.

steps.action: Process the data: convert DAS phase to strain, correct cycle skipping with a moving median, integrate strain to displacement, stack shots, and remove the geophone response using the manufacturer's poles and zeros.
steps.quote: The strain data were integrated spatially over one gauge length centred on the measurement point, to obtain displacement at each sensing channel.

steps.action: Compare uncoupled and coupled fibre shot profiles, raw and normalized: the uncoupled fibre shows signal over about 10-16 m, DAviS-coupled sections are strong, the carpet degrades the signal, and the sandbag gives a local signal.
steps.quote: The stacked shots at 1 m (Figure 3b) of the coupled fibre show a stronger signal visible at distances of 0–25 m

steps.action: Offer explanations for two anomalies: the sandbag-segment arrivals (fibre orientation and directivity, SH waves, uniform strain) and the near-source noise (interrogator fringe tracking versus a complicated source nearfield).
steps.quote: This might be caused by the optical phase travelling over multiple fringes

steps.action: Compare coupled DAS displacement with vertical and estimated horizontal geophone waveforms and shot sections: phases match, amplitude differs by up to a factor of 1.1-2.0, and correlation is 0.46 with the horizontal versus 0.21 with the vertical.
steps.quote: The coupled DAS record is roughly in phase with the estimated horizontal geophone component from 0.0–0.2 s.

steps.action: Estimate the P-wave velocity structure by two-layer refraction analysis of first arrivals (330 m/s over 1.2 m, then 1100 m/s down to 6.2 m).
steps.quote: P-wave velocities are determined using a two-layer refraction method using first arrivals (Figure 6).

steps.action: Check the flat-layer assumption using shots at opposite ends of the array.
steps.quote: [...] at opposite ends of the linear array shows no evidence for dipping layers.

steps.action: Estimate the S-wave velocity structure from f-v beamforming of a single shot, forward-modelling the fundamental and three higher modes with Computer Programs in Seismology.
steps.quote: we find S-wave velocities of 185 m/s in the shallowest 6.2 m

steps.action: Compare f-v results across sensors: vertical geophones show mainly the fundamental mode, estimated horizontal and coupled DAS show fundamental and higher modes, uncoupled DAS shows a weak fundamental mode; both data sets give the same 1-D structure.
steps.quote: the estimated horizonal geophone component and coupled DAS record show both a fundamental mode and higher modes

steps.action: Estimate an empirical DAS-to-horizontal-displacement response function by spectral division, using coherence of at least 0.8 between 7.8 and 62.5 Hz to select records and the reliable band.
steps.quote: We find that the signals are highly coherent between 7.8 Hz and 62.5 Hz, with average coherence values typically higher than 0.8.

steps.action: Compare SNR and wave-type recovery with published buried-fibre studies, noting that this study is dominated by surface waves while those studies found strong body waves.
steps.quote: we find similar variability in SNR and retrieval of P-, S- and surface waves in comparison to previously published work.

steps.action: List four rival explanations for the DAS-geophone amplitude mismatch: poorly estimated tilted-geophone response, fibre and sheathing elasticity, imperfect coupling, and gauge-length spatial averaging.
steps.quote: There are several possible explanations for the difference in amplitude between the estimated horizontal geophone record and the DAS record.

steps.action: Derive the expected effect of gauge-length averaging from the minimum wavelength (about 4 m at 185 m/s and 50-70 Hz) and conclude that little spatial aliasing is expected.
steps.quote: we do not expect much spatial aliasing based on our gauge length of the DAS system.

steps.action: Keep the claim that uncoupled fibre records the nearfield, while DAviS or sandbag coupling records P, S and Rayleigh waves to at least 23 m with phase matching horizontal motion; the amplitude mismatch is left unresolved.
steps.quote: Better coupling via a DAviS coupler or sandbag, improves the SNR, allowing observation of P-waves, S-waves and Rayleigh waves

tree.answer: Fidelity of surface-laid DAS fibre recordings under different coupling strategies
Yes: strain recorded directly and compared with co-located geophones
Characterize coupling strategies and the DAS response to ground motion
No rivals before the data; post hoc explanations for near-source noise and amplitude mismatch
Only one rival (spatial aliasing) given an explicit expectation; the others are not separated
Conditions set by the authors in the field (coupling type, geophone tilt, shot positions)
Partly: tilt-angle uncertainty and a reversed-shot check; single site, single shot for the response function
Coupled DAS phase agrees with the estimated horizontal motion; amplitude mismatch up to a factor of 2

end.claim: A surface-laid fibre records hammer-source waves within about 10 m even when uncoupled, and DAviS-pinned or sandbag-weighted fibre records P, S and Rayleigh waves to at least 23 m with phase matching the inline horizontal ground motion, but with amplitudes differing by up to a factor of two.

decisive_move.sentence: The comparison of coupled DAS displacement with the horizontal component estimated from tilted geophones (waveforms, shot sections, f-v) is what establishes that the fibre records inline horizontal motion with correct phase.

gates.evidence: The acquisition was designed as a comparison of coupling strategies, not directed by a stated hypothesis. The DAS-geophone comparison could have failed (phase disagreement), but no acceptance criteria were fixed in advance. The coherence threshold of 0.8 is applied after inspecting the data (p. 473). Nothing is reported as pre-registered.

imports.item: Phase-OTDR DAS interrogator based on an imbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometer with arctan phase demodulation
Standard SMF-28 tight-buffer telecom optical fibre used as the sensor
Hanning-window cross- and auto-spectral estimation and coherence for an empirical transfer function (Oppenheim & Schafer; Bendat & Piersol)

limits: The paper contains no explicit 'first' or 'previously unknown' statements; the closest is 'One of the most surprising observations is that a completely uncoupled fibre can be used to record the ground motion' (p. 474), so novelty_claims is empty. The experiment is a single site with one substrate (grass on clay-rich soil). The empirical response function rests on one shot location (23 m), and the authors say averaging over more shots would improve it (p. 474). The reference horizontal motion is estimated from tilted, uncalibrated geophones rather than measured with three-component sensors, so the amplitude comparison has a large acknowledged uncertainty. The sandbag and carpet were placed on the corner and W-E segment, which confounds coupling type with fibre orientation (acknowledged, p. 474). Rival explanations for the near-source noise and the amplitude mismatch are listed but not tested, except the spatial-aliasing expectation. Sub-claims: the 1-D Vp/Vs model (pp. 472-473) is an estimate given without uncertainty (estimate_with_resolution only loosely); the empirical response function is estimate_with_resolution over 7.8-62.5 Hz with error bars (p. 473). Coder inferences: the controlled field set-up was coded as F on mode instruments rather than F on hypothesis (the codebook names only laboratory and live-event cases), and the DAS-versus-geophone comparisons were treated as control checks against a reference rather than as replication. Data are available on request only (p. 476).

disagreements.target: Martin et al. (2017) and Zhu et al. (2021), active-source studies with buried telecom fibre
disagreements.support: Their DAS records showed weak surface waves but good body waves and reflections, whereas these surface records are dominated by surface waves; the authors attribute the difference to depth, source, structure and coupling.
disagreements.quote: This contrasts with our study, which was dominated by surface wave energy with little evidence for reflections.
